After a breakup you can feel like a project someone gave up on. This verse says the most important work in you is still in progress and was never theirs to finish.

skip.why: Well-meaning people send the marriage passages to the freshly single as a kind of “next time.” Not now. The person is grieving, not shopping. Psalm 147:3 is about the wound; send that.

whatToSay: “That’s awful. I’m sorry.” Then don’t say anything about how they are better off.
“Want to come over and not talk about it?” Distraction is a real gift in the first week.
Be the friend who doesn’t say “I never liked him.” They may get back together, and they will remember.
Check in on the first weekend, the first holiday, and the day you know the ex has moved on.
Don’t say: “God has someone better for you.” Maybe. Not the point, and not yours to promise.
howToUse: Psalm 147:3 the first night. Lamentations 3:22–23 in the mornings. If you are sending one to a friend, keep the note to a sentence and skip anything that sounds like advice.

faq.q: Does the Bible say anything about breakups?
faq.a: Not about dating breakups directly; the world it was written in did not have them in this form. It says a great deal about broken hearts, being left, and beginning again, which is what a breakup is made of. Psalm 147:3 and Lamentations 3 were written for exactly this shape of loss.

faq.q: Is it okay to be angry at the person?
faq.a: The psalms are full of anger at people who hurt the writer, and they were kept in the Bible. Bring the anger to God rather than to the ex’s phone. Ephesians 4:26 is the guidance: be angry, and don’t let it settle in and rot.

faq.q: What verse can I send a friend after a breakup?
faq.a: Psalm 147:3 with one line: “This is a real loss and I’m sorry. This came to mind.” Nothing about the ex, nothing about the future.

title: Bible Verses After a Divorce
h1: Bible verses after a divorce
label: After a divorce
description: Bible verses for someone going through or recovering from divorce: a crushed spirit, restored years, rising after a fall, and a new creation. No lectures.
intent: The person is divorcing or divorced and often feels judged by church people. They want comfort and a path forward, not a debate.
intro: Divorce is grief with paperwork, and often with an audience. People going through it tell me the hardest part is not the loss; it is the sense that the loss is also a verdict. These verses were chosen with that in mind. None of them are about the rules of marriage. They are about a crushed spirit, years that felt wasted, falling and rising, and a new creation. Whatever anyone has said to you, this page is not going to say it.

verses.why: Near to the brokenhearted; saves those who have a crushed spirit. “Crushed” is the right word for divorce: not just sad, but flattened. The verse promises nearness in exactly that state. It does not ask what happened or whose fault it was. That is why it is first.

“Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning.” The Hebrew pictures weeping as a guest who lodges overnight. David wrote it looking back on a season he did not think he would survive. It does not say the night is short. It says it ends, from someone who has been through one.

“I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten.” Said to a nation after a plague stripped the fields bare. Divorce can make years feel eaten: the wedding, the plans, the photographs. This is the one verse in the Bible that speaks directly to years that feel wasted, and it says they are not beyond restoring.

“When I fall, I will arise. When I sit in darkness, Yahweh will be a light to me.” Micah says it to enemies who are enjoying his defeat. If your divorce has an audience, this is the verse for it. Not “I did not fall.” Fell, and rising anyway.

“If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away.” Paul is talking about what happens to a person in Christ, not about divorce specifically, and that is the point: your identity is not “divorced.” It is new, and the newness does not have a prior condition.

“Don’t remember the former things. Behold, I will do a new thing.” Written to exiles who could not stop remembering. It is not a command to forget the marriage; it is a refusal to let the marriage be the last thing that ever happens to you. Some days that is hard to believe. The verse says it anyway.

Come to me, all who are weary. Divorce is exhausting in a way outsiders do not see: lawyers, custody calendars, splitting a life into two piles. Jesus offers rest, and then a yoke that fits. Not less to carry, but a way of carrying it with someone gentle.

skip.why: “I hate divorce” gets sent to divorcing people by relatives who mean it as truth-telling. Whatever it means in context (it is addressed to men abandoning their wives), it is not comfort, and the person has heard it. Psalm 34:18 is what they have not heard enough.

whatToSay: “I’m on your side. I don’t need the details.”
“Which weekends are the kids gone? I’ll put something on the calendar.” The empty weekends are the worst part.
If they are still going to church, sit with them. If they have stopped, don’t make it an issue.
Don’t ask what happened. If they want you to know, they will tell you.
Don’t say: “Have you tried counseling?” or “God hates divorce.” Both arrive as verdicts.
howToUse: Psalm 34:18 first. Joel 2:25 when the wasted-years feeling hits. Micah 7:8 for the day you have to see people. If someone sends you a verse that sounds like a judgment, you are allowed to delete it.

faq.q: Does God still love someone who is divorced?
faq.a: Yes, without qualification. Nothing in the Bible ranks the loved by marital status, and Jesus’ longest recorded conversation with an individual was with a woman who had been married five times (John 4). He offered her living water, not a lecture.

faq.q: What verse can I send a friend going through a divorce?
faq.a: Psalm 34:18 or Joel 2:25, with one line: “I’m on your side.” Nothing about what happened, nothing about the ex, nothing about marriage.

faq.q: Can I still serve or lead in a church?
faq.a: That depends on the church, not on the Bible’s view of you. If yours has made you feel disqualified as a person, that is worth talking through with someone outside it.

title: Bible Verses When You Are Afraid of the Future
h1: Bible verses when you are afraid of the future
label: Afraid of the future
description: Bible verses for fear about what comes next: uncertainty, dread about tomorrow, waiting for the other shoe to drop. Days already written, and a hand that goes ahead.
intent: The person is anxious about what is coming: a decision, a season, life in general. They want verses about the future that don’t promise a specific outcome.
intro: Fear of the future is the most common fear in the Bible, if you count how often God says “don’t be afraid” to people about to walk into something. These verses were chosen for the dread that has no single cause: the sense that the other shoe is going to drop. None of them tell you what is coming. They tell you who is going ahead, and how much of it you are asked to carry today.

verses.why: Jesus’ last line in a long argument about worry: tomorrow will worry about itself. He does not say tomorrow will be easy. He says today’s trouble is enough, and that carrying tomorrow’s on top of it only doubles the load. Fear of the future is mostly the habit of paying for things twice. This verse is permission to pay once, on the day.

Said to exiles who had every reason to dread what was coming: I am with you, I will strengthen you, I will uphold you with my right hand. The future in that verse is not described. The company in it is. That is the shape of every honest promise about tomorrow.

Trust with all your heart, don’t lean on your own understanding, and he will make your paths straight. Straight, not easy, not visible in advance. The verse is about direction rather than outcome, which is the only kind of guidance the future actually allows for.

“I will instruct you and teach you in the way which you shall go. I will counsel you with my eye on you.” Written by David after a season of hiding something and then owning it. The last phrase is a picture of attention, not surveillance. Someone is watching how you go.

“When you pass through the waters, I will be with you.” When, not if. The verse assumes the waters. It is one of the few promises about the future in the Bible that is completely honest: hard things are coming, and you will not go through them alone.

Be strong and courageous, said three times in nine verses to a man about to lead a nation across a river into hostile country, which suggests he was not feeling either. The reason given is not Joshua’s ability. It is “Yahweh your God is with you wherever you go.” Courage in this verse is a conclusion from company.

“In your book they were all written, the days that were ordained for me, when as yet there were none of them.” The psalmist finds it a comfort that his days were known before any of them happened. Read it as a statement that the future is not unwritten chaos. Someone has read ahead.

skip.why: The obvious verse for the future, and it was written to exiles about a return seventy years out. Quoted as “God has a great plan for my next year,” it sets people up for a fall. Its real promise, that God’s intentions are good even across a long wait, is sturdier and is what Isaiah 43:2 says more plainly.

whatToSay: “What’s the specific thing you’re dreading?” Naming it usually shrinks it.
“What do you need to do today?” Not this month. Today.
“I’ll be there for the thing on Thursday.” Fear of the future shrinks when someone else is in it.
Don’t say: “It’ll all work out.” You don’t know that, and they know you don’t. Say: “Whatever happens, you won’t be alone in it.”
howToUse: Matthew 6:34 in the morning, as a rule for the day. Psalm 139:16 at night. If the fear has a specific object, a diagnosis, a job, a decision, there are pages for each of those, and they will fit better.

faq.q: Does the Bible say not to plan for the future?
faq.a: No. Proverbs praises the ant for storing food, and Jesus tells a story about counting the cost before building a tower. The warning is against anxiety about the future, not preparation for it. Plan, then hand the plan over.

faq.q: What if my fear is about something real, like losing my job?
faq.a: Then it is not irrational, and the verses do not ask you to pretend it is. Matthew 6 was said to people who genuinely might not have food tomorrow. The instruction is about which day’s trouble you carry, not about whether the trouble is real.

faq.q: What verse can I send someone who is scared about what’s coming?
faq.a: Isaiah 43:2 with one line: “When, not if. You won’t go through it alone.”

title: Bible Verses for Estrangement From an Adult Child
h1: Bible verses when your adult child has cut you off
label: Estranged from a child
for: a parent estranged from an adult child
description: Bible verses for parents whose adult child has gone low or no contact: for the silence, the waiting, and the door left open. Comfort, not ammunition.
intent: A parent’s grown child has stopped speaking to them. The parent is grieving, ashamed, and often bewildered. They want comfort, not ammunition, and not a plan to force contact.
intro: Estrangement from an adult child is a grief nobody brings casseroles for. There is no funeral, no card, and often no one to tell, because the first question is always “what happened,” and you may not fully know. These verses were chosen for the parent in that silence. None of them is about winning the child back, and none of them should be sent to the child. They are about how to keep a heart open across a distance you did not choose and cannot close by yourself. One thing I will say plainly, because it is the seed of estrangement in so many families now: if the distance began when your child came out, the verses below still hold, and so does this: the relationship is worth more than winning, and no doctrine requires you to choose between your child and your faith. There is a section for that below.
safety: If your child has asked for space, the most loving and most hopeful thing you can do is honor it. Scripture will not help you if it becomes a way around a boundary. If the silence has become despair, or you are drinking or not sleeping because of it, please talk to a counselor; this is one of the hardest griefs there is, and it is worth professional help.

verses.why: The father in Jesus’ story does not go get his son. He waits, and he watches the road, and when the son appears “while he was still far off,” he runs. Every estranged parent knows the road-watching part. The verse does not promise the son comes back on a schedule; the story has already skipped an unknown number of years. What it shows is the posture: not chasing, not closed, ready. That is the whole page in one verse.

Near to the brokenhearted. Estrangement breaks a heart slowly, in a way friends stop asking about after the first year. This verse does not require you to know what went wrong or to have fixed it. The nearness is a response to the breaking, not to the reconciliation.

“Can a woman forget her nursing child? Yes, these may forget, yet I will not forget you.” Spoken to Israel, who felt abandoned by God. Read it two ways. It is a comfort to a parent who cannot stop thinking about a child who seems to have forgotten them. And it is a reminder that the child is engraved on God’s hands too, which means you are not the only one holding them.

“If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.” Two honest qualifiers. Sometimes it is not possible right now. And peace takes two; your part is only your part. This verse gives permission to stop trying to control the other half, which is the part that is making you sick.

“My soul, wait in silence for God alone, for my expectation is from him.” Not from the child. The most painful thing about estrangement is that your hope is pinned to someone else’s decision. This psalm moves the hope somewhere steadier, without saying the wish for reconciliation is wrong.

Cast all your worries on him, because he cares for you. The reason clause is the point: he cares about this particular worry, the one you don’t say at church because someone will ask what you did. You are allowed to hand it over every day for years. The verse does not have an expiration.

A time to keep silence, and a time to speak; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain. Estrangement is a season of refraining, and this passage says such seasons exist in the design and are not permanent by definition. It does not tell you how long. It tells you that silence can be a season rather than a verdict.

skip.why: Please do not send this to your child, and do not let anyone send it to them for you. It is true, and used this way it is a weapon, and it will confirm the reason for the distance. If contact ever reopens, it will be because the child felt safe, not because they felt commanded.

whatToSay: To yourself: “I don’t have to understand all of it to be at peace with my part of it.”
If you write to the child, once: “I love you. I’m not going anywhere. I’ll respect what you’ve asked.” Then respect it. No verse, no guilt, no questions.

If your child is gay or trans and the distance began there: “I love you. I don’t want to lose you. I may still be working some things out, and none of that is bigger than you.” Then stop sending verses about it. They have read them all, and each one arrives as the reason for the distance.
To a friend who asks: “We’re not in touch right now. It’s painful. I’d rather not go through the details.” You do not owe anyone the story.
If the child reaches out: answer warmly, briefly, and without relitigating anything. Let them set the pace.
Don’t say to the child: “After everything I did for you.” It may be true. It ends the conversation.
howToUse: Luke 15:20 for the posture. Psalm 62:5–6 when you catch yourself checking the phone. Romans 12:18 when you want to fix it. These are for you; none of them is for the child. If you are the adult child reading this page, the same verses hold for you, and Psalm 27:10 is yours in particular.

faq.q: Should I keep reaching out?
faq.a: If your child has asked for no contact, honor it; reaching out anyway teaches them the boundary won’t hold, and it delays the day they might feel safe enough to try again. If they have not said, one brief, warm, no-pressure message on a birthday or holiday, with no questions in it, is generally right. Then stop and wait.

faq.q: Is estrangement a sin on their part, or mine?
faq.a: This page is not going to adjudicate that, and neither should anyone who does not know the whole story. Adult children who go no contact almost always experience it as self-protection, whether or not the parent sees it that way. Romans 12:18 gives you the only assignment you can carry out: your part.

faq.q: What if I don’t know what I did?
faq.a: That is common and it is agony. If the child ever tells you, listen without defending, even if you see it differently. In the meantime, a counselor who works with estrangement can help you look at your part honestly without drowning in it.

faq.q: My child came out, and that is when it broke. What do I do?
faq.a: First, the honest thing: your child likely experienced your reaction as a verdict on who they are, whatever you meant. The way back, if there is one, does not run through winning the argument. It runs through them believing they are safe with you. Nothing in Scripture requires you to choose your child over your faith or your faith over your child; the God who is “a father of the fatherless” did not put that choice in front of you, and people who tell you it is that choice are adding to the text. What Jesus consistently did with the people his religious culture kept at arm’s length was eat with them. Start there, if they let you. And if you need someone to talk this through with, look for a counselor or a pastor who has walked families through it rather than one who will rehearse the argument with you; your child has heard it.

faq.q: I’m the adult child. Is there anything here for me?
faq.a: Yes. Psalm 27:10, “when my father and my mother forsake me, then Yahweh will take me up,” and Psalm 34:18. Distance can be the right choice and still grieve you. Nothing on this page is meant to push you toward contact you are not safe to have.

title: Bible Verses After Losing Someone to Suicide
h1: Bible verses after losing someone to suicide
label: Loss to suicide
for: someone who lost a loved one to suicide
description: Bible verses for grief after a suicide: for the questions no one can answer, the guilt that isn’t yours, and the darkness that Scripture does not pretend away.
intent: Someone died by suicide. The person is a family member or close friend, often carrying guilt and unanswerable questions, sometimes told cruel things by religious people.
intro: Grief after a suicide is grief with a second wound: the why, the what-ifs, and sometimes a religious voice saying something unforgivable about where the person is now. This page will not do that. The Bible knows what despair sounds like; it kept a psalm that ends in darkness, and it records a prophet asking to die. These verses are for the people left, and they are honest that some questions will not be answered here.
safety: If you have thought about ending your own life since the loss, please tell someone today. In the US, call or text 988; elsewhere, your country has a line and a search for “crisis line” will find it. Suicide loss raises the risk for those left behind, and asking for help is not weakness; it is what you would want the person you lost to have done.

verses.why: Near to the brokenhearted; saves those who have a crushed spirit. This is the first verse because it does not ask a single question. It does not ask what happened, whether you saw the signs, or what the person believed. It says God is near to exactly the state you are in, and, read plainly, it says the same about the state your loved one was in.

The only psalm that never turns toward hope. It begins in darkness and ends in darkness, and it was kept in the Bible on purpose. Read it and you will know that Scripture does not flinch from what your loved one may have felt, and does not require you to feel better on schedule. God can be cried out to from the bottom, and the psalm proves it by being there.

Elijah, one of the greatest prophets, sits under a tree and asks God to let him die. God’s response is not a rebuke. It is food, sleep, and a touch, twice. If you are wondering how God regards someone who wanted to die, this is the closest the Bible comes to showing you: with tenderness, and practical care. It is also permission for you to eat and sleep.

“If I say, ‘Surely the darkness will overwhelm me,’ even the night will be light about me. The darkness doesn’t hide from you.” The psalmist has been trying to find a place beyond God’s reach and cannot. For a family asking where their loved one was in the last hours, this verse says: not outside the light. Not hidden. Seen.

“He won’t break a bruised reed. He won’t quench a dimly burning wick.” Said of the servant God sends, and applied by Matthew to Jesus. A person who dies by suicide was a bruised reed, a wick burning low. This verse is how God handles those. Let it answer the voices, inside or outside your head, that say otherwise.

Paul’s list of what cannot separate us from God’s love begins with death and includes “things present” and “things to come.” It does not have an exception for how a death happened. If you take one verse to the hardest question, take this one, and read it as it is written, without adding a clause.

Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. Suicide loss often comes with a sense that you are not allowed to mourn normally, that there is shame around it. Jesus puts no condition on the blessing. Mourning is mourning. The comfort is promised to all of it.

skip.ref: Any verse used to say where the person is now
skip.why: People will quote 1 Corinthians 6:19 or Exodus 20:13 at you, sometimes gently, to explain that the person is lost. The Bible nowhere says that a person’s last act decides their standing with God, and Romans 8:38–39 says the opposite. If someone says it to you, you do not have to answer. If it is playing in your own head, read Isaiah 42:3 out loud.

whatToSay: “I don’t have any answers. I’m here, and I loved him too.”
Say the person’s name. Suicide loss makes people afraid to, and the silence is its own cruelty.
Don’t ask how. Don’t ask whether they saw it coming. If they want to tell you, they will.
Show up at the six-month mark, when the shock has worn off and the questions have started. That is usually the hardest stretch.
Don’t say: “They’re at peace now,” “It was selfish,” or anything about where they are. You do not know, and it is not the comfort.
howToUse: Psalm 34:18 first. Isaiah 42:3 when the shame gets loud. Romans 8:38–39 when someone says something unforgivable. If you are a pastor, please read Psalm 88 at the service; the family needs to hear that the Bible has a place for what happened.

faq.q: Does the Bible say people who die by suicide go to hell?
faq.a: No. That teaching came from church tradition centuries later, not from Scripture, and most churches have abandoned it. The Bible records several suicides without commentary on the person’s eternal state, and Romans 8:38–39 states that nothing, including death, separates from God’s love. Anyone who tells you otherwise is speaking for themselves.

faq.q: Could I have stopped it?
faq.a: Almost everyone left behind asks this, and the honest answer from people who study suicide is that it is far less predictable and preventable than hindsight makes it feel. Guilt is a normal part of this grief, not evidence. A grief counselor or a survivors-of-suicide-loss group can help you set it down; the verses can keep you company while you do.

faq.q: What verse can I send someone who lost a family member to suicide?
faq.a: Psalm 34:18, with one line: “I don’t have any answers. I loved him too, and I’m here.” Nothing about where he is. Nothing about why.

title: Bible Verses After Losing a Sibling
h1: Bible verses after losing a brother or sister
label: Lost a sibling
description: Bible verses for the death of a brother or sister: the loss of the person who shared your childhood, from David’s lament to Mary at her brother’s tomb.
intent: A brother or sister has died. The person is often overlooked in the grief (attention goes to parents or spouse) and wants verses that fit a sibling specifically.
intro: A sibling is the only person who remembers your childhood from the inside. When they die, the grief is often overlooked; the attention goes to the parents, or the spouse, and the brother or sister is expected to be the strong one. The Bible has two of the most honest sibling griefs ever written: David’s lament for Jonathan, and Mary saying to Jesus, “if you had been here, my brother would not have died.” These verses start there.

verses.why: David’s lament for Jonathan: “I am distressed for you, my brother. Your love to me was wonderful.” It is raw, personal, and it was written down and kept. If you have not been given room to grieve a sibling, this is the Bible giving it to you. David does not say Jonathan is in a better place. He says he is distressed, and that the love was wonderful.

Mary falls at Jesus’ feet: “if you had been here, my brother would not have died.” It is an accusation and a grief in one breath, and Jesus does not correct her. He is troubled, and he weeps. Whatever you are saying to God about your brother or sister, Mary said it first, and the response was tears, not a lecture.

Near to the brokenhearted. Sibling loss can leave you as the family’s designated strong person, and this verse does not ask you to be strong. It asks nothing at all. The nearness comes to the broken state, not to the composed one.

“A brother is born for adversity.” The proverb is about what a sibling is for: the one who shows up when things go wrong. Losing that person means losing your backup. Read it as a description of what you had, and as a grief for it, not as a demand to replace it.

“Two are better than one. If they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls.” For many people the sibling was the “two.” This passage names the specific loss: not just the person, but the one who lifted you up. That is why it hurts in the way it does.

“My flesh and my heart fail, but God is the strength of my heart.” For the stretch after the funeral, when you are managing your parents’ grief and your own has no room. The psalm allows the failing. It just says something holds underneath it.

Death, mourning, crying, and pain gone. The last page. For a sibling who shared the first pages with you, the promise that the story has an ending written down can be a real comfort, or can be too soon. Read it when you are ready, not before.

skip.why: Not in the Bible, not how the Bible describes people, and it makes God the one who took your brother. Psalm 34:18 says what is actually true: God is near to you in the loss, not the cause of it.

whatToSay: “You lost your brother. I’m so sorry.” Say it to the sibling directly; most people only say it to the parents.
“What was she like when you were kids?” Nobody else can tell those stories now.
“How are you doing, not your parents, you?” The sibling is often managing everyone else’s grief.
Don’t say: “At least your parents still have you.” It makes the sibling responsible for filling a gap that cannot be filled.
howToUse: 2 Samuel 1:26 if you need permission to grieve out loud. John 11:33–35 if you are angry at God. Ecclesiastes 4:9–10 to name what exactly was lost. If you are comforting a sibling, address them, not the family.

faq.q: Why does no one ask how I’m doing?
faq.a: Sibling grief is called “disenfranchised” for a reason: culturally, the spouse and parents are seen as the primary mourners, and the brother or sister is expected to support them. Your grief is real and the Bible’s own example, David for Jonathan, treats it as one of the deepest there is.

faq.q: What verse is good for a sibling’s funeral?
faq.a: 2 Samuel 1:26 if you are speaking as the sibling; John 11:25–26 for the service; Psalm 23 for the graveside. Ecclesiastes 4:9–10 works if the two of you were close in a way the room knows about.

faq.q: What can I send someone whose brother or sister died?
faq.a: Psalm 34:18, addressed to them by name, with: “You lost your brother, and I’m so sorry. This came to mind.” Make it about their loss, not their parents’.

title: Bible Verses After Losing a Pet
h1: Bible verses after losing a pet
label: Lost a pet
description: Bible verses after the death of a dog, cat, or other animal: sparrows that don’t fall unnoticed, a God who preserves man and animal, and a grief allowed to be real.
intent: A pet has died. The person feels the grief is real but suspects it is not allowed, and wants to know whether the Bible has anything for it.
intro: People apologize for grieving a pet, which tells you something about the grief: it is real enough to need excusing. The Bible does not require the apology. It says God made the animals and called them good, that he preserves man and animal alike, that a sparrow does not fall without the Father, and that the righteous care for the life of their animals. These are the verses for the empty spot by the door.

verses.why: “Aren’t two sparrows sold for an assarion coin? Not one of them falls to the ground apart from your Father.” Jesus says it to reassure people about their own worth, and the argument only works if the sparrow’s fall really is noticed. It is. If the smallest bird does not die unseen, neither did the animal that slept at the foot of your bed for twelve years.

“Yahweh, you preserve man and animal.” One line, and it puts animals inside God’s care in the same breath as people. Not the same as people. In the same sentence. The psalm is about how far God’s love and faithfulness reach, and the answer includes the creatures.

God made the animals, “and God saw that it was good.” Before there were people, there were animals, and God’s verdict on them was the same as on everything else he made. Your dog or cat was one of those. The grief you feel is grief for something God called good.

“A righteous man respects the life of his animal.” The Bible’s only verse about pet care, and it treats caring well for an animal as a mark of a good person. If you are second-guessing the last decisions, the vet visits, the day you had to choose, this verse is on your side: the care was the righteous thing, all the way to the end.

“Yahweh is good to all. His tender mercies are over all his works.” All his works. The psalm is one long list of God’s kindness, and this line refuses to draw a boundary around who it covers. Whatever you believe about where animals go, this says they were never outside his mercy.

Paul says creation itself will be “delivered from the bondage of decay into the liberty of the glory of the children of God.” The verse is about all of creation being included in what is coming, not just people. Christians have read it as hope for the animals for a long time. It is not a proof. It is a door left open.

“He heals the broken in heart, and binds up their wounds.” No qualification about what broke it. If you are embarrassed by how much this hurts, this verse is not. Binding a wound takes time; it does not skip the pain, and it does not ask why.

skip.why: “Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward, and the spirit of the animal goes downward?” gets quoted both to comfort and to correct. It is the Teacher of Ecclesiastes asking a question, in a book built on not knowing. It settles nothing, and it is not what a grieving pet owner needs. Matthew 10:29 is.

whatToSay: “I’m sorry about Max. He was a good dog.” Say the name. Say it was a good animal.
Don’t say: “It was just a dog” or “You can get another one.”
If they had to choose euthanasia: “That was the kind thing. You did right by her.” They are replaying it.
A card with the animal’s name on it means more than people expect.
howToUse: Matthew 10:29 if you need to know the loss was seen. Proverbs 12:10 if you are second-guessing the end. For a child who has lost a pet, Genesis 1:25 and Psalm 145:9 are simple enough to read together.

faq.q: Do pets go to heaven?
faq.a: The Bible does not answer directly. It says creation as a whole is included in what God is restoring (Romans 8:21, Isaiah 11:6–9), and it never says animals are excluded. Christians have disagreed for centuries and most have landed on hope. What Scripture does say clearly is that God made them, called them good, and notices when they fall.

faq.q: Is it wrong to grieve a pet this much?
faq.a: No. Grief is proportional to attachment, and a pet is often the one creature that was with you every single day. Psalm 147:3 puts no condition on which broken hearts get bound up.

faq.q: What can I say to a child whose pet died?
faq.a: “God made Biscuit and said she was good, and he knows exactly where she is.” Then read Matthew 10:29 together. Let them cry. Don’t rush to a new pet.

title: Bible Verses for Panic and Panic Attacks
h1: Bible verses for panic
label: Panic
description: Short Bible verses to hold onto during a panic attack, and passages for the fear of the next one. Jesus in the storm, a rock higher than you, and a mind kept.
intent: The person has panic attacks, or is in one, or is afraid of the next. They need verses short enough to say while breathing, not paragraphs.
intro: In a panic attack you cannot read a paragraph. You can hold about five words. So the first verses here are short enough for that: Peace, be still. When I am afraid, I will trust in you. The later ones are for afterward, when the fear of the next one sets in. None of them is a treatment. Panic responds well to real help, and the safety note below means it.
safety: Panic attacks are common and very treatable, and you deserve treatment, not just verses. A doctor or therapist can teach you tools that work in minutes. If you are having chest pain, difficulty breathing that does not ease, or symptoms you have not had before, get medical care now rather than assuming it is panic.

verses.why: Jesus, woken in a boat that is filling with water, says three words to the storm: “Peace! Be still!” Panic feels exactly like that boat. This is the verse to say on the exhale, over and over, because it is short enough to say while breathing and because the one who said it was speaking to a storm that stopped. It is not a technique. It is a name to call.

“When I am afraid, I will put my trust in you.” Eleven words, and honest ones: not “I am not afraid.” David writes it while captured by enemies. It is a sequence to repeat: fear arrives, trust is chosen, fear loosens, and the sequence runs again. In a panic attack that repetition is the whole prayer.

“When my heart is overwhelmed, lead me to the rock that is higher than I.” The psalmist does not claim to be able to climb it. He asks to be led. Panic is the heart overwhelmed, precisely, and this is a prayer for during it: not to fix it, but to be taken somewhere higher than the wave.

“We won’t be afraid, though the earth changes, though the mountains are shaken into the heart of the seas.” A panic attack is the earth changing under you. This psalm was written for a city under siege and it is honest that the shaking is real. The refuge is “very present,” meaning here, now, before the shaking stops.

“You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you.” The word for “steadfast” means propped up, leaned. It does not say your mind will never race. It says a racing mind can be leaned, again and again, onto something that holds. For the days between attacks, when you are bracing for the next one.

Paul’s instruction, written from custody, is a practice rather than a feeling: every specific fear becomes a specific request, with thanks. The peace that follows is described as a guard posted at the door of your mind. After an attack, this is what to do with the fear of the next one: hand it over, item by item, and let the guard stand.

“God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.” The word for fear here is timidity, a shrinking back. It is not a verse that says panic is a spiritual failure; Paul wrote it from prison to a frightened young man. It says the panic is not who you are, and the self-control is a gift, not a demand.

skip.why: Someone will tell you the Bible says “fear not” 365 times, one for each day, as if the count settles it. Every one of those is said to a frightened person by someone offering presence, not issued as a rule. Psalm 56:3 is what the Bible actually sounds like about fear: when I am afraid, I will trust. Not: don’t be.

whatToSay: During: “You’re safe. I’m right here. Breathe out slowly.” Say one short thing and then be quiet.
Don’t say: “Calm down” or “There’s nothing to be afraid of.” Both make it worse.
After: “That was hard. Want to walk?” Movement helps, and it changes the subject without dismissing it.
If they’ve never seen a doctor about it: “This is really treatable. Want me to come with you?”
howToUse: Pick one short verse, Mark 4:39 or Psalm 56:3, and make it yours before the next attack, so it is already in your mouth when you need it. The longer ones are for afterward. And please, if you have not, talk to a doctor; the verses will keep you company through treatment, and treatment works.

faq.q: Is panic a lack of faith?
faq.a: No. Elijah, David, and Paul all describe states that sound a great deal like panic, and none of them is rebuked for it. Panic is a body’s alarm system misfiring. Faith is what you lean on while it does; it is not a switch that turns the alarm off.

faq.q: What is the shortest verse for a panic attack?
faq.a: “Peace! Be still!” from Mark 4:39. Three words, said by Jesus to a storm. Say it on the exhale.

faq.q: Should I pray instead of taking medication?
faq.a: Both, if your doctor recommends medication. Nothing in the Bible sets prayer against medicine; Luke was a physician and Paul told Timothy to take something for his stomach. Pray, and take what helps.

title: Bible Verses While Waiting for Bad News
h1: Bible verses while waiting for bad news
label: Waiting for bad news
description: Bible verses for the dread before the call: a biopsy, a verdict, a layoff list. Passages for a heart kept steady before the news, not after.
intent: The person is waiting for something they expect to be bad: a diagnosis, a court decision, a layoff, a phone call. They want verses for the dread itself.
intro: Waiting for bad news is its own kind of suffering, and in some ways the worst: nothing to do, nothing to fight, every phone call a possible verdict. These verses were chosen for the dread, not the news. Some were written by people who then got the bad news anyway. That is what makes them trustworthy. They are not a promise that the call will be good. They are for the person by the phone.

verses.why: “He will not be afraid of evil news. His heart is steadfast, trusting in Yahweh.” A verse about bad news, written for the time before it arrives. The person described does not know it will be fine. His heart is steady because it rests on something other than the outcome, which is the only steadiness available while the phone has not rung.

“Though the fig tree doesn’t flourish, nor fruit be in the vines … yet I will rejoice in Yahweh.” Habakkuk has just been told that invasion is coming, and it is. This is the Bible’s clearest statement of trust that does not depend on the news being good: even if it is all bad, even if the fields are empty, still. Read it before the call, so it is already said.

“I am still confident of this: I will see the goodness of Yahweh in the land of the living. Wait for Yahweh. Be strong, and let your heart take courage.” David has spent a whole psalm talking himself steady, and this is where he lands: waiting, said twice, with courage in the middle. Waiting is a decision you make more than once, sometimes several times before noon.

“It is good that a man should hope and quietly wait for the salvation of Yahweh.” Written in a ruined city by someone who had already received every piece of bad news there was. If he can say quiet waiting is good, it is not naive to say it now. Quiet does not mean calm. It means not filling the silence with rehearsed catastrophes.

“My soul, wait in silence for God alone, for my expectation is from him. He alone is my rock and my salvation, my fortress. I will not be shaken.” David moves his expectation off the outcome and onto God. Then the careful phrase: not greatly shaken. The psalm allows for wobbling. It just says you will not be toppled.

Don’t be afraid, for I am with you. Five promises in a breath, to exiles who then stayed in exile a long time. The verse does not promise the news is good. It promises a grip that does not depend on it. That is the promise for the waiting room.

Tomorrow will worry about itself. The mind produces a full year of consequences from one pending call, and then lives through all of them before lunch. Jesus’ instruction is to carry today only. Today, you are waiting. That is the whole assignment for today, and it is enough, and tomorrow will have its own provision when it comes.

skip.why: “Plans to prosper you and not to harm you” is the verse people send while you wait, and it implies they know the news will be good. They don’t, and you know they don’t. Habakkuk 3:17–18 is the honest one: even if it isn’t, still.

whatToSay: “I know you’re waiting. I’m not going to ask. I’m just here.”
“Whatever it is, you won’t hear it alone. Call me right after.”
Offer to be there when the call comes, or to sit with them the night before.
Don’t say: “I’m sure it’s nothing.” Say: “Whatever it is, we’ll deal with it together.”
howToUse: Habakkuk 3:17–18 the night before. Psalm 112:7 the morning of. Matthew 6:34 every time the mind runs ahead. If the news comes and it is bad, the pages for a cancer diagnosis, job loss, and grief are here, and they were written for after.

faq.q: How do I stop imagining the worst?
faq.a: You probably can’t stop it; you can decline to follow it. Matthew 6:34 is the discipline: when the mind runs to tomorrow, name today’s one task, which is waiting, and come back to it. Say Psalm 112:7 out loud. Move your body. Repeat as needed; it is a practice, not a switch.

faq.q: Is it okay to pray for a specific outcome?
faq.a: Yes. Jesus prayed for the cup to pass, and then said “not my will.” Ask plainly for the news you want. Habakkuk 3 is the second half of that prayer: and if not, still.

faq.q: What verse can I send someone waiting for a diagnosis or a decision?
faq.a: Psalm 112:7, with: “I know you’re waiting. I’m not going to ask. I’m just here.” That is the whole message.

title: Bible Verses for Starting a New Job
h1: Bible verses for starting a new job
label: New job
description: Bible verses for the first day and first month of a new job: nerves, wanting to do well, and working for someone other than the boss.
intent: The person is starting a new job and is nervous, or wants to send a verse to someone who is. They want encouragement that is not a promise of promotion.
intro: The first week of a new job is a strange mix of hope and dread: you wanted this, and you have no idea where the bathroom is. These verses are for that week and the month after, when you are still proving yourself. None of them promises you will be a star. They say who you are working for, who goes ahead of you, and how to hand the outcome over.

verses.why: “Yahweh himself is who goes before you. He will be with you. He will not fail you nor forsake you. Don’t be afraid.” Moses says it to Joshua about to take over a job Moses had done for forty years. Someone going ahead of you into the building is exactly the reassurance a first day needs. It does not say the job will be easy. It says the room is not empty when you walk in.

“Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men.” Paul wrote it to household servants who had no career and no say in who they worked for. To them, of all people, he says: your work is for the Lord and he sees it. That reframes the new boss, the new team, and the fear of being judged. You have one audience, and he is generous.

Be strong and courageous, said three times to a man starting the hardest job in the nation, which suggests he did not feel either. The reason given is not Joshua’s ability. It is “Yahweh your God is with you wherever you go,” including the new office.

“Commit your deeds to Yahweh, and your plans shall succeed.” Proverbs describes how life usually goes, so read this as a pattern rather than a contract: work handed over tends to go better than work clutched. Practically, it is a habit for the first month: at the start of each day, hand the day over, then do it.

“Let the favor of the Lord our God be on us. Establish the work of our hands.” A prayer, not a promise, and the right one for a new job: not “make me impressive,” but let what I do here last. The psalm is Moses reflecting on how short life is, so the request is for work that matters, not work that dazzles.

“My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest.” God’s answer to Moses when Moses was afraid to lead without him. Read it for the evenings of the first week, when you come home wired and doubting. The presence goes in with you, and the rest is part of the deal.

“I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.” The verse everyone sends on the first day, and it was written by Paul about being content whether he had plenty or nothing. So read it the way he meant it: not “I will crush this,” but “whatever this job turns out to be, I can be all right in it.” That is a better thing to carry in on day one.

skip.why: On more first-day cards than any verse, and written to exiles about a return seventy years off. Sent to someone starting a job it reads as “God got you this for your prosperity,” which sets them up badly if the job is hard. Deuteronomy 31:8 says the true thing: someone goes ahead of you.

whatToSay: “You’re going to be good at this. Text me after.”
“Nobody expects you to know anything the first week. Ask every question.”
Check in on Friday of the first week, not Monday. Monday they’re fine; Friday they’re tired and doubting.
Don’t say: “Don’t be nervous.” Say: “Nervous is right. It means you care.”
howToUse: Deuteronomy 31:8 in the car before you walk in. Colossians 3:23 when the new boss is difficult. Proverbs 16:3 as a morning habit for the first month. If you are sending one, Deuteronomy 31:8 with a line about texting you after.

faq.q: What is a good verse for a first day at work?
faq.a: Deuteronomy 31:8: someone goes ahead of you into the building. If you want something shorter, Joshua 1:9.

faq.q: What if the new job turns out to be a mistake?
faq.a: Then Colossians 3:23 still holds: the work is for the Lord regardless of the employer, and that gives you dignity while you decide what to do. The starting-over page is here if you need it.

faq.q: What can I write in a card for someone’s new job?
faq.a: Deuteronomy 31:8 or Psalm 90:17 with one line: “Proud of you. Go get it.” Skip Jeremiah 29:11; everyone else will send it.

title: Bible Verses After Losing a Child
h1: Bible verses after losing a child
label: Lost a child
for: a parent who lost a child
description: Bible verses for parents who have lost a child, at any age, including miscarriage and stillbirth. Passages that do not explain the loss or rush the grief.
intent: A parent’s child has died: an infant, a child, a teenager, an adult child, or a pregnancy. They want verses that do not explain, minimize, or promise a reason. Or someone is trying to comfort such a parent and is terrified of saying the wrong thing.
intro: There is no page on this site I have written more slowly. The death of a child is the loss the Bible itself treats as beyond words: it records a mother who refuses to be comforted, and God does not correct her. None of these verses explains why. None of them says it was for the best. What they say is that the child was known, was carried, is not forgotten, and that the grief is allowed to be as large as it is, for as long as it is. If you are here for someone else, the section on what to say is short on purpose.
safety: If you are a parent who has lost a child and you have thought about ending your own life, please tell someone today: a friend, your doctor, or a crisis line (in the US, call or text 988). Wanting to be with your child is one of the most common feelings in this grief, and saying it out loud to someone who can help is not a betrayal of them.

verses.why: “Rachel weeping for her children. She refuses to be comforted for her children, because they are no more.” This is in the Bible. A mother who will not be consoled, and the text does not scold her; it records her. Matthew quotes the verse after the children of Bethlehem are killed. If everyone around you is trying to comfort you and you cannot receive it, Scripture has a place for exactly that. You are allowed to refuse comfort for a while. Rachel did.

Near to the brokenhearted; saves those who have a crushed spirit. First for almost every grief on this site, and here most of all, because it asks nothing. It does not ask you to trust a plan, find a reason, or be strong for the other children. The nearness is a response to the breaking. That is the whole promise, and it is the only one that fits the first months.

David, after his infant son dies: “Can I bring him back again? I will go to him, but he will not return to me.” He had fasted and wept for seven days while the child lived. Afterward he says the plainest thing a bereaved father has ever said, and it holds grief and hope in one sentence: the child is not coming back, and I am going to him. It is the Bible’s clearest statement about where a small child is.

“He will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom.” The shepherd’s smallest sheep are the ones he carries, not leads. This is an image rather than an argument, which is what the days after can bear. For a child of any age, the picture of being gathered up and carried close is the one parents tell me they hold onto.

“In your book they were all written, the days that were ordained for me, when as yet there were none of them.” For a child whose life was short, or never began outside the womb, this verse says the life was whole: every day written, none of them accidental. It does not say why there were so few. It says each one was known and counted.

Jesus, about children: “in heaven their angels always see the face of my Father.” He says it to warn adults against despising little ones, and the reason he gives is that the little ones are already attended in heaven. Read it plainly, without adding to it. It is the verse for a parent who needs to know their child is not alone where they are.

Parents pushing forward, disciples pushing back, and Jesus indignant on the children’s behalf: “Allow the little children to come to me.” Then he takes them in his arms and blesses them. Read it without commentary at a child’s funeral. It is the picture of what welcome looks like, and it is the one that most parents can bear to hear.

“You put my tears into your container. Aren’t they in your book?” Ancient mourners kept tears in small bottles; the psalmist imagines God doing the same, keeping every one. Months in, when the grief has become invisible to everyone around you, this verse says it is seen and counted, not fixed and not explained. That is the only kind of comfort that lasts.

Two words: Jesus wept. At a tomb he was about to empty. He knew what he would do and he wept anyway, because the loss was real and Mary was weeping. If you are wondering whether your grief is a failure of faith, or being told it is, this is the answer. Grief is the right response to death, and Jesus had it.

Every tear wiped away, and death, mourning, crying, and pain gone. The last page. For some parents this is the only verse that helps; for others it is unbearable for a long time, because it is about later and the child is gone now. Both are right. It is placed last here for that reason. Read it when you are ready.

skip.ref: Job 1:21 (“Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away”)
skip.why: Job says it about his own children, in his own grief, and he is allowed to. It is not for anyone else to say to a bereaved parent, and it makes God the one who took the child. Isaiah 40:11 says what is true and bearable: the lamb is gathered and carried. The other line to leave out is Romans 8:28; in this grief, “all things work together for good” cannot be heard as anything but “this was for the best,” and it wasn’t.

whatToSay: Say the child’s name. Every time. For years. Parents say the worst part is when the world stops saying it.
“I’m so sorry. There are no words, and I’m not going to try to find them. I’m here.”
If the child was born still or died before birth: “She was your daughter. I’m so sorry you lost her.” Use the name if there is one. Do not say “at least you can try again.”
Bring food, mow the lawn, take the other children to school. Do it without asking, for months.
Mark the birthday and the day of death in your calendar and say something on both, every year.

Never say: “God needed an angel,” “Everything happens for a reason,” “He’s in a better place,” “At least you have your other children,” or anything that begins with “at least.” Never ask what happened.
howToUse: If you are the parent: one verse, kept for a season. Many parents keep Isaiah 40:11 or Psalm 139:16. Jeremiah 31:15 is for the days you cannot receive anything, and it is enough to know it is there. If you are a friend or a pastor: read Mark 10:14–16 or Isaiah 40:11 at the service and say nothing after it. Presence over words, for as long as it takes.

faq.q: Where is my child now?
faq.a: The Bible does not lay out a doctrine of infant death, and I will not pretend it does. What it gives is David’s “I will go to him,” Jesus taking children in his arms and saying the kingdom belongs to such as these, and his word that their angels see the Father’s face. Christians across every tradition have read those together as assurance that a child who dies is with God. That is what I believe. I would not send anyone to argue the point with you.

faq.q: Is there anything for a miscarriage or stillbirth?
faq.a: Yes, and it is the same grief, not a smaller one. Psalm 139:13–16 says the child was knit together and every day was written, even when the days were few. 2 Samuel 12:23 is David after the death of an infant. If people around you are treating it as less than a death, this page is not, and neither is Scripture.

faq.q: My child was an adult. Is this page for me?
faq.a: Yes. A parent burying an adult child is still burying a child, and the order of things is still wrong. Isaiah 40:11 and 2 Samuel 12:23 do not depend on the child’s age. The loss-of-a-spouse and loss-of-a-parent pages may help for your child’s family, but this one is yours.

faq.q: What can I send a parent who lost a child?
faq.a: Isaiah 40:11 and the child’s name, and nothing else: “Thinking of you and of Ellie today.” Then again next month. Then on her birthday. The sending matters more than the verse.

title: Bible Verses for Addiction and Recovery
h1: Bible verses for addiction and recovery
label: Addiction
description: Bible verses for the person fighting an addiction, in recovery or not yet: Paul’s honest line about doing what he hates, a way of escape, and falling seven times.
intent: The person is struggling with drinking, drugs, gambling, pornography, or another compulsion, or is in recovery and afraid of relapse. They want honesty, not shame, and not a promise that a verse will cure it.
intro: If you are fighting an addiction, you have probably already been handed verses as weapons. This page is not that. The Bible’s most honest sentence about compulsion was written by the apostle Paul: “what I hate, that I do.” He is not describing weakness of faith; he is describing what it is like to be a person. These verses are for the fight, for the morning after, and for the long stretch of recovery where nothing dramatic happens and you just keep going.
safety: A verse is not a treatment. If you are physically dependent on alcohol or a drug, stopping suddenly can be dangerous; talk to a doctor first. Recovery programs, counselors, and treatment centers exist and they work, and going to one is not a failure of faith. In the US, the SAMHSA helpline is 1-800-662-4357, free and confidential, any hour.

verses.why: “I don’t practice what I desire to do; but what I hate, that I do.” Paul, an apostle, describing the split between what he wants and what he does. This is the first verse because it says the thing every addicted person knows and is ashamed of: knowing better does not stop you. Scripture puts that sentence in the mouth of one of its heroes, on purpose, so nobody reading it would think they were the only one.

“What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me?” Then: thanks be to God through Jesus Christ. Paul does not resolve the split by trying harder; he resolves it by looking outside himself. This is the honest shape of recovery: the admission first, then the hand reached for. It is very close to what the first steps of any twelve-step program say, and that is not an accident.

The verse behind “God won’t give you more than you can handle,” and for once the real meaning is the useful one: no temptation is unique to you, and there is always a way of escape. Not a way to never be tempted; a door out of the specific moment. Recovery is learning where the door is and walking through it one more time than you don’t.

“A righteous person falls seven times and rises again.” The proverb does not say the righteous don’t fall. It says the difference is getting up. If you have relapsed, this is the verse: the falling is in the definition of the person who makes it, and the counting stops mattering.

Mercies new every morning, written in a ruined city. For recovery this is practical: the day counter can reset, and the mercy resets too. Yesterday is not deducted from today. A person who slipped last night and is reading this at breakfast is exactly who the verse is for.

David’s prayer after the worst thing he ever did: “Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.” Note the verb. He does not ask to be cleaned up; he asks to be made new, which is a different request and the only realistic one. Say it as a prayer when you have nothing else.

“If the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.” Jesus, to people who insisted they had never been slaves to anyone. The freedom on offer is real, and it does not arrive all at once for most people; it arrives the way recovery does, in mornings. Hold the verse as the destination, not as a test you are failing today.

skip.why: “I can do all things” gets taped to the fridge in early recovery, and when the person slips it becomes proof they failed at faith too. Paul wrote it about being content while hungry in prison. Proverbs 24:16 is the recovery verse: falls seven times, rises again.

whatToSay: “I’m proud of you for today.” Just today.
“Want to grab coffee instead?” Offer the alternative, not the lecture.
If they relapse: “Okay. What do you need right now?” Not “again?”
Go to the open meeting if they invite you. Presence beats advice.
Don’t say: “Just pray about it,” or “Where’s your faith?” Both make God one more thing they’re failing.
howToUse: Romans 7:15 for the shame. Proverbs 24:16 for the morning after. Lamentations 3:22–23 taped where you brush your teeth. And a program, a counselor, or a doctor alongside all of it; the verses keep you company through treatment, they don’t replace it.

faq.q: Is addiction a sin?
faq.a: The Bible names drunkenness among things to avoid, and it also describes, in Paul’s own voice, the experience of being unable to do what you know is right. Both are true and neither is the useful question at 6 a.m. The useful question is what to do today, and the Bible’s answer is get up, reach out, and go to whoever can help.

faq.q: Does prayer cure addiction?
faq.a: Some people describe a moment where the craving lifted. Many faithful people do not get that and recover the ordinary way: treatment, meetings, honesty, time. Pray, and go to the meeting. Nothing in Scripture sets prayer against medicine or counseling.

faq.q: What verse can I send someone in recovery?
faq.a: Proverbs 24:16 with one line: “Proud of you for today.” Never Philippians 4:13, and never anything that sounds like a test.

title: Bible Verses When Someone You Love Is an Addict
h1: Bible verses when someone you love is an addict
label: A loved one’s addiction
for: someone whose loved one is an addict
description: Bible verses for the parent, spouse, or friend of an addict: for the waiting, the boundaries, the 3 a.m. phone, and the difference between love and rescue.
intent: The person’s child, spouse, parent, or friend is addicted. They are exhausted, scared, and guilty, and they have been told opposite things about whether to help or step back.
intro: Loving an addict is a grief that keeps not ending. You watch someone you love disappear a little at a time, you learn what the 3 a.m. phone means, and everyone has an opinion about what you should do. These verses are for you, not for them. None of them tells you whether to pay the bail or change the locks; that is between you, your counselor, and a group like Al-Anon. What they offer is a place to put the fear, and permission to have a life while you wait.
safety: If you are in danger from the person, or your children are, your safety comes before anything on this page. Al-Anon, Nar-Anon, and family programs exist for people in exactly your position; they are free, they are everywhere, and the people in them will understand you without an explanation.

verses.why: Cast all your worries on him, because he cares for you. You have been carrying this person, and the verse is not about them; it is about you, and the reason clause is the point. He cares about the one doing the carrying. You are allowed to set the worry down every night, and pick it up again in the morning if you must, and set it down again.

The father in Jesus’ story does not go to the far country and drag his son home. He waits, he watches the road, and when the son turns up on his own, he runs. Every parent of an addict knows the road-watching. The story does not say how many years it took. What it shows is the posture: not chasing, not closed, ready. You cannot make the turning happen. You can be the kind of house someone comes back to.

“My soul, wait in silence for God alone, for my expectation is from him.” Not from the person. The most exhausting thing about loving an addict is having your hope pinned to someone else’s next decision. This psalm moves your hope somewhere steadier without asking you to stop loving them.

Near to the brokenhearted, and the crushed. A loved one’s addiction crushes slowly, in a way friends stop asking about. The nearness in this verse does not depend on the person getting better. It is a response to your state, now.

“If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.” Two honest qualifiers. Sometimes it is not possible. And only part of it is up to you. This verse is permission to stop managing the half that was never yours, which is usually the half making you sick.

A very present help in trouble, though the earth changes and the mountains shake. The phone rings at 3 a.m. and the earth changes; that is exactly the psalm’s picture. The refuge is available while it is shaking, not after, and it does not require you to have handled the call well.

“Can a woman forget her nursing child? Yes, these may forget, yet I will not forget you.” Read it for yourself when you feel forgotten by everyone. Read it again for the person you love: they are engraved on those hands too, which means you are not the only one holding them, and you can let go for a night.

skip.why: “Train up a child in the way he should go” gets handed to parents of addicts as an accusation: you must have trained him wrong. It is a proverb about how things usually go, not a guarantee, and it has broken a lot of good parents. Luke 15:20 is what to hold instead.

whatToSay: To yourself: “I didn’t cause it, I can’t control it, I can’t cure it.” Say it until you believe it.
To the person, once, when they’re sober: “I love you. I’m not going anywhere. And I won’t help you hurt yourself.”
To a friend in this: “Come to a meeting with me.” Not “have you tried…”
Don’t say to a parent: “Have you thought about tough love?” They have thought about everything.
howToUse: 1 Peter 5:7 at night when you put the phone on the nightstand. Psalm 62:5–6 when you catch yourself waiting for the call. Luke 15:20 when you want to drive to the far country. And a meeting for you, this week.

faq.q: Should I keep helping, or step back?
faq.a: The Bible will not answer that for your situation, and anyone who quotes a verse at you as if it does is guessing. It does say, plainly, that peace takes two and only your part is yours (Romans 12:18). A counselor or an Al-Anon group can help you find the line between love and rescue in your specific case.

faq.q: I feel like it’s my fault.
faq.a: Almost everyone in your position does. Proverbs 22:6 is not a guarantee, and children raised well become addicts every day. Psalm 34:18 does not ask whose fault it was. Neither should you, for a while.

faq.q: What verse can I send someone whose son or daughter is an addict?
faq.a: 1 Peter 5:7 with one line: “I know you’re carrying a lot. Coffee Thursday? We don’t have to talk about it.”

title: Bible Verses for Dementia and Alzheimer’s
h1: Bible verses for dementia and Alzheimer’s
label: Dementia
for: someone with dementia, or the family
description: Bible verses for a parent or spouse with dementia or Alzheimer’s, and for the family: being remembered when you can’t remember, and carried to gray hairs.
intent: A parent or spouse has dementia. The person is grieving someone who is still alive, exhausted from caregiving, and wants verses that speak to memory loss without pretending it isn’t happening.
intro: Dementia is a long goodbye to someone who is still in the room. The person may not know your name; you know theirs, and you carry both halves of the relationship. The Bible does not have a verse about Alzheimer’s. It has a great deal about being remembered by God when memory fails, and about being carried to old age and gray hairs. These verses are for the person, while they can still hear them, and for the family, for the long stretch after that.
safety: If you are the caregiver, you are at high risk of burning out, and the disease does not care how strong you are. Respite care, adult day programs, and the Alzheimer’s Association helpline (1-800-272-3900, US, any hour) exist for you. Accepting help is not abandoning your parent.

verses.why: “Even to old age I am he, and even to gray hairs I will carry you.” God to Israel, about a whole life. For a parent who no longer knows the day, this is the verse to read aloud, because the carrying does not depend on the person knowing who is carrying them. Being held does not require remembering that you are.

“You know my sitting down and my rising up. You perceive my thoughts from afar.” The psalm is about being completely known by God. When a person can no longer hold their own history, this says someone else is holding it, all of it, every day they have forgotten. Nothing is lost that God knew.

“Don’t reject me in my old age. Don’t forsake me when my strength fails.” An old man’s prayer, kept in the Bible. It gives words to the fear underneath dementia, for the person and for the family: that when you are no longer useful or sharp, you will be set aside. The psalmist asks not to be, and the rest of the psalm is his confidence that he won’t.

“If we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he can’t deny himself.” A person with dementia may lose the ability to pray, to recognize a hymn, to say they believe. This verse says God’s faithfulness is not conditioned on ours holding up. The relationship is kept from his side.

“Can a woman forget her nursing child? Yes, these may forget, yet I will not forget you.” Read this one twice. Once for the parent who has forgotten you: they are engraved on those hands. Once for yourself: the verse admits that people forget, even the ones who loved you most, and it does not blame them.

As a father has compassion on his children. For he knows how we are made; he remembers that we are dust. For the family, this is the honest one: frailty is known and held, not explained. And it says God remembers our frame when we cannot remember anything.

Come to me, all who labor and are heavily burdened. For the spouse who has become a full-time nurse, for the daughter who sleeps in the chair. The rest on offer is a burden that fits, carried alongside someone gentle. Caregiving is the load; this verse is about the yoke.

skip.why: Sent to families as an explanation. There is no good in dementia to work toward, and the verse read that way sounds like the disease was for the best. Isaiah 46:4 says what is true: carried to gray hairs, whether or not anyone understands why.

whatToSay: To the person: their name, often, and yours, without quizzing. “Hi Mom, it’s Sarah.” Not “Do you know who I am?”
Read the psalm they knew. Sing the hymn. Long-term memory outlasts everything else, and the familiar words reach them.
To the caregiver: “Go home and sleep. I’ll sit with her tonight.”
Don’t say: “At least she’s not in pain,” or “She wouldn’t want to live like this.” Neither is yours to say.
howToUse: Isaiah 46:4 at the bedside, read aloud, whether or not they seem to follow. Psalm 139:1–4 for yourself when the grief of being unrecognized hits. Matthew 11:28 for the caregiver. The caregivers sheet in the Comfort Kit has more for the one in the chair.

faq.q: Does a person with dementia still have faith?
faq.a: Faith is not a memory test. 2 Timothy 2:13 says God remains faithful when we cannot. Chaplains who work in memory care describe people who cannot say their own name singing every word of a hymn. The relationship is kept from God’s side, and that is the whole point of grace.

faq.q: Is it wrong to grieve someone who is still alive?
faq.a: No. It has a name, anticipatory grief, and it is common and exhausting. Psalm 34:18 does not require a funeral. Let people bring you casseroles now.

faq.q: What can I send someone whose mother has Alzheimer’s?
faq.a: Isaiah 49:15–16 with one line: “She’s engraved on his hands even on the days she doesn’t know yours. Thinking of you both.”

title: Bible Verses for Infertility
h1: Bible verses for infertility
label: Infertility
description: Bible verses for infertility and trying to conceive: Hannah weeping at the temple, a psalm that starts “how long,” and a Bible that does not look away.
intent: The person or couple is trying to conceive and can’t, often through treatment, and is surrounded by baby announcements and well-meaning verses about God’s timing. They want honesty.
intro: Infertility is a monthly grief in a world that keeps announcing pregnancies. The Bible is full of women who could not conceive, and it does not tidy their stories: Hannah weeps so hard at the temple that a priest thinks she is drunk. Some of those women eventually had children; this page will not promise you will. What it will do is refuse to look away, and give you a psalm that starts with “how long.”
safety: If the grief has become despair, or the treatment cycle has left you unable to function, a counselor who works with infertility can help, and so can a support group like RESOLVE. This is a recognized loss, and you are allowed to get help for it.

verses.why: Hannah, “in bitterness of soul,” weeping and praying at the temple while her rival mocks her. This is the Bible’s most honest picture of infertility, and the first thing to notice is that she is allowed to be bitter. She does not compose herself before she prays. She prays like that, and she is heard like that. If you cannot pray nicely about this, you are in good company.

“How long, Yahweh? Will you forget me forever?” A psalm that begins with the question infertility asks every month, kept in the Bible as a prayer. You are allowed to ask it out loud. The psalm turns toward trust by the end, but it does not skip the question, and neither should you.

Near to the brokenhearted. The verse does not ask why the heart is broken, and it does not require a baby announcement to be true. For the negative test, the failed cycle, the baby shower you couldn’t attend, and the friend who announced in the group text. The nearness is a response to the breaking, not a reward for coping.

“We don’t know how to pray as we ought, but the Spirit himself makes intercession for us with groanings which can’t be uttered.” For the days when you have prayed the same thing so many times you have no words left. The verse says the wordlessness is itself prayer, carried by someone else.

“He settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother of children.” Included with care: it is a line about what God has done for some, in a psalm of praise, not a promise about your outcome. Some people find it cruel in this season and some find it the only hope they have. Read it if you can; skip it if you can’t. Both are allowed.

“God remembered Rachel, and God listened to her.” After years, after her sister had son after son, after Rachel had said “give me children or I die.” The verb is remembered. Whatever the outcome of your story, this verse says the waiting was not unwitnessed and the asking was heard.

“Sing, barren, you who didn’t give birth.” Said to Israel, about a nation that would have more children than it could count. The context is national, and I will not pretend it is a personal promise. What carries is the idea that barrenness is not the end of a story in Scripture; it is where several of the biggest ones begin.

skip.why: “Children are a heritage from the Lord” and “plans to prosper you” get sent to couples in fertility treatment as encouragement, and both land as a verdict: everyone else got the heritage, and the plans are apparently for other people. Psalm 13 is what to send: how long, asked honestly.

whatToSay: “I’m so sorry. That must be so hard every month.” Then stop.
Tell them before you announce a pregnancy, privately, so they don’t find out in a group text.
“I’d love to have you at the shower, and I’ll completely understand if you can’t.”
Don’t say: “Just relax,” “Have you tried…,” “Maybe it’s not God’s plan,” or “You can always adopt.” They have heard all four this week.
howToUse: 1 Samuel 1:10–11 when you need permission to be bitter. Psalm 13 as a prayer, out loud. Romans 8:26 when you have no words. Psalm 113:9 only if it helps; put it down if it doesn’t.

faq.q: Is infertility a punishment?
faq.a: No. The Bible’s barren women include Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, and Elizabeth, some of the most honored people in it. Jesus explicitly rejects the idea that suffering is a verdict on the sufferer (John 9:3). Anyone suggesting otherwise is wrong.

faq.q: Does the Bible promise I will have a child?
faq.a: No. It records that some barren women did, and it promises that God hears and remembers. Those are different things, and I would rather tell you the truth than hand you Psalm 113:9 as a guarantee.

faq.q: What can I send a friend going through infertility?
faq.a: Psalm 34:18 and one line: “I’m thinking of you this month. No need to reply.” Say nothing about timing, plans, or adoption.

title: Bible Verses for Someone in Prison
h1: Bible verses for someone in prison, and for their family
label: In prison
for: someone in prison, or their family
description: Bible verses for someone in jail or prison, and for the family outside: Paul writing from a cell, Joseph in the pit, and a Bible that remembers prisoners.
intent: Someone is incarcerated, awaiting trial, or just released, or the person is the parent, spouse, or child of someone who is. They want verses that fit a cell and do not lecture.
intro: A surprising amount of the New Testament was written from a cell. Paul wrote Philippians, the most joyful letter in the Bible, while chained and awaiting a verdict. Joseph was in a pit and then a prison for years before anything changed. The Bible remembers prisoners, tells the church to visit them, and does not treat a sentence as the end of a person’s story. These verses are for the person inside, and for the family carrying it on the outside, who often get less sympathy than anyone.
safety: If you are the family: the shame you feel is common and it is not yours. Prison Fellowship and similar ministries have programs for families, and children of incarcerated parents in particular need someone to say out loud that they did nothing wrong.

verses.why: Paul, in chains, to a church he loves: the things that happened to me have turned out for the progress of the Good News. He is not pretending prison is pleasant. He is saying it is not wasted. Written from custody, this is the most credible thing in the Bible about a sentence not being the end of usefulness.

“Remember those who are in bonds, as bound with them.” A direct instruction to the church: don’t forget prisoners, and feel it as if it were you. For someone inside, this says you are supposed to be remembered. For the family, it is the verse to hand a church that has gone quiet.

“I was in prison, and you came to me.” Jesus lists visiting prisoners among the things done to him personally. Whatever you did, the man in the visiting room is, by Jesus’ own words, someone worth a visit. And for the family who keeps making the drive: he counts it.

Joseph, years after his brothers sold him and years after Potiphar’s prison, to those same brothers: “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.” He does not say the prison was good. He says something came of it that he could not have seen from inside. It is a verse for later, and knowing it exists helps now.

“Bring my soul out of prison, that I may give thanks to your name.” David wrote this hiding in a cave, so the prison was his circumstances, but the words have been prayed in actual cells for three thousand years. It is a prayer you can say as written.

Jesus’ first sermon, quoting Isaiah: sent to proclaim release to the captives. Whatever your parole date, this is what he said he came for. Read it plainly; it is not only spiritual, and it is not only literal. It is both, and it was the first thing he said about his work.

Near to the brokenhearted, and the crushed. For the wife at home, the mother who visits monthly, the kid who tells the school his dad is “away.” The family of a prisoner carries a shame that is not theirs and gets less sympathy than almost anyone. The verse does not ask what the sentence was for.

skip.why: Quoted at prisoners and their families as a reminder that the system is right. Whatever it means, it is not comfort, and the person has already been sentenced. Hebrews 13:3 is the verse the church is told to act on, not that one.
