whatToSay: Write. A letter is the most valuable thing a person inside can receive, and most people stop writing after the first month.
To the family: “How are you doing? Not him. You.”
To a child with an incarcerated parent: “You didn’t do anything wrong, and your dad still loves you.”
Don’t ask what they did. If they want you to know, they’ll tell you.
howToUse: Philippians 1:12–14 for the person inside, with the reminder that Paul wrote it there. Psalm 142:7 as a prayer to say as written. Hebrews 13:3 to hand a church that has stopped calling. For the family, Psalm 34:18.

faq.q: Can God forgive what I did?
faq.a: The Bible’s answer is not abstract: it includes a murderer (Moses), an adulterer who arranged a killing (David), a man who persecuted Christians to death (Paul), and a thief forgiven on the cross with hours to live. None of them earned it. Romans 8:1: there is now no condemnation for those in Christ. That is the whole answer.

faq.q: How do I explain this to my kids?
faq.a: Simply and truthfully, at their level, and with one sentence that they will need to hear many times: you did nothing wrong. Programs for children of incarcerated parents exist and are worth finding; the shame these kids carry is heavy and it is not theirs.

faq.q: What verse can I write to someone in prison?
faq.a: Philippians 1:12–14, with: “Paul wrote this in chains. Thinking of you, and I’ll write again next month.” Then write again next month.

title: Bible Verses for a Financial Crisis
h1: Bible verses for a financial crisis
label: Money crisis
description: Bible verses for bankruptcy, losing the house, or not making rent: the birds that are fed, a prayer for enough, and provision versus prosperity.
intent: The person is in real financial trouble: bankruptcy, foreclosure, eviction, medical debt, or a business failing. They are ashamed and afraid, and they have heard prosperity verses that made it worse.
intro: A financial crisis is fear with a due date. It is also one of the loneliest troubles, because people hide it, and because the church has often confused God’s promise of provision with a promise of prosperity. This page keeps them separate. The Bible says the birds are fed; it does not say the mortgage is guaranteed. These verses are for the night you run the numbers again and they still do not work.
safety: Please also talk to someone who handles money for a living: a nonprofit credit counselor, a bankruptcy attorney (many give free consultations), or your lender before you miss a payment rather than after. Bankruptcy is a legal tool, not a moral failure, and it exists because the Bible’s own law had a year of release for debts.

verses.why: “Don’t be anxious, saying, ‘What will we eat?’” Jesus says it to people who genuinely might not eat tomorrow, not to people worried about a portfolio. The promise is that the Father knows you need these things, and that the kingdom comes first. It is a promise of provision, not prosperity: enough, not plenty. Read it as written and it holds.

“Give me neither poverty nor riches. Feed me with the food that is needful for me.” The Bible’s most honest prayer about money, and the only one that asks for enough rather than more. If you don’t know what to pray for when the numbers don’t work, pray this, as written.

“My God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory.” Paul wrote it to thank a church for sending money to him in prison, so the “need” he had in mind was real and specific. It is not a blank check. It is a promise from a man who had just received exactly enough.

“Be free from the love of money, content with such things as you have, for he has said, ‘I will in no way leave you.’” The promise of presence sits inside a sentence about money, on purpose. When the house goes, the presence does not. That is the actual guarantee, and it is a better one.

“I have been young, and now am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his children begging for bread.” An old man’s testimony, not a law of nature; some righteous people have gone hungry. Read it as one long life’s observation: he watched a lot of people go through a lot of trouble and saw them provided for in the end, and he wrote it down.

“The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, says Yahweh of Armies.” Said to people rebuilding a temple with no budget. For someone whose crisis is that the money is gone, this is a reorientation: it was never the thing holding you up. Whoever owns the silver is not worried about your account.

“Commit your way to Yahweh. Trust also in him, and he will do this.” The Hebrew for commit means roll, like rolling a load off your back. Financial fear is a load you carry at 3 a.m. This is the verse for rolling it off, tonight, and rolling it off again tomorrow.

skip.ref: Malachi 3:10 (“test me in this”) and any prosperity verse
skip.why: “Bring the whole tithe and see if I will not open the windows of heaven” gets used to tell people in crisis that giving more will fix it. Whatever it meant to Israel, using it that way on a family facing foreclosure is cruel. Proverbs 30:8–9, a prayer for enough, is what the Bible actually sounds like about money.

whatToSay: “I don’t need the details. What would help this week?” Then do the specific thing: groceries, gas, the electric bill paid directly.
Invite them to things that don’t cost money, and don’t make a point of it.
Don’t say: “Have you tried budgeting?” or “God will provide” as a way to end the conversation. Provide something.
howToUse: Proverbs 30:8–9 as the prayer. Hebrews 13:5 at night. Matthew 6:31–33 in the morning, read as enough-not-plenty. And a credit counselor or attorney this week; the verses will keep you company through the paperwork.

faq.q: Is bankruptcy a sin?
faq.a: No. The Old Testament law required debts to be released every seven years (Deuteronomy 15) and property returned in the Jubilee; the idea of a fresh start from debt is biblical before it is legal. Use the tool if you need it, and don’t let anyone shame you for it.

faq.q: Did God promise to make me prosperous?
faq.a: He promised to provide what you need, and the Bible is careful about the difference. Jesus and Paul both lived without money. The verses that get quoted as prosperity promises are almost all about enough, read in context.

faq.q: What can I send someone losing their house?
faq.a: Hebrews 13:5, with: “The house isn’t the thing holding you up. I’m around this weekend if you need hands.”

title: Bible Verses After an Accident
h1: Bible verses after an accident
label: After an accident
description: Bible verses after a car accident, a fall, a fire, or a disaster: for the shock, the hospital, the survivor’s guilt, and the long recovery nobody sees.
intent: Someone was in an accident, or survived a fire or disaster. They are in shock, hurt, or grieving, and may feel guilty for surviving or for causing it.
intro: An accident divides life at a single second, and the mind replays that second for months. These verses are for the days after: the hospital, the shock, the guilt that may not be rational and is real anyway, and the long recovery after the visitors stop. None of them explains why it happened. The Bible’s own answer to a collapsed tower killing eighteen people was that they were no worse than anyone else, and that is the honest answer here too.
safety: Flashbacks, nightmares, and jumpiness are normal after an accident, and if they persist past a month they have a name and a treatment. Tell your doctor. And if the accident was your fault and you cannot stop replaying it, a counselor is the right next call, before any verse.

verses.why: A very present help in trouble, though the earth changes and the mountains shake. Written for a city under siege, it describes exactly what an accident feels like: the ground giving way. The refuge is present, meaning now, while the shaking is still happening.

“Yahweh will keep you from all evil. He will keep your soul. He will keep your going out and your coming in.” People in accidents sometimes read this bitterly, since it didn’t keep them from the crash. Read the middle line: he will keep your soul. The psalm’s promise is about what cannot be lost, and the accident proved that the body can be. That is a harder and truer comfort.

When you pass through the waters, when you walk through the fire. When, not if. Isaiah writes it to people who have already been through the worst. The verse assumes the fire and promises company in it. For someone who literally walked out of one, it lands differently.

“Yahweh my God, I cried to you, and you have healed me.” David, looking back at a time he thought he would die. For the long recovery, physical therapy, the surgery after the surgery, this is the verse to say in advance, as a hope, until it becomes a memory.

Near to the brokenhearted, and the crushed. For survivor’s guilt: the friend who lived when someone else didn’t, the driver who walked away. The verse does not ask whose fault it was. The nearness is a response to the crushing, not a verdict on the cause.

“There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus.” If you caused the accident, or believe you did, this is the verse, and it is not a loophole. It does not say what happened was fine. It says condemnation is not what is waiting for you. What is waiting is a way through, and that starts with saying what happened to someone.

Come to me, all who labor and are heavily burdened. Recovery is labor: the appointments, the pain, the paperwork, the fear of getting back in a car. The rest on offer is a burden that fits, carried alongside someone gentle.

skip.ref: Romans 8:28 and “everything happens for a reason”
skip.why: After a crash that killed someone, or maimed someone, “all things work together for good” sounds like the accident was for the best, and it wasn’t. Jesus, asked about eighteen people killed by a falling tower, refused to give a reason (Luke 13:4–5). Psalm 46:1 is what to send: present help, no explanation.

whatToSay: “I’m so glad you’re here.” Say it plainly. Survivors need to hear it.
“What do you need this week? Rides, meals, someone to sit with you at PT?” Then do it for months, not days.
If someone else died: say their name. Survivors are afraid to.
Don’t say: “It could have been worse,” or “At least…,” or anything about reasons. Don’t ask for the details.
howToUse: Psalm 46:1–3 the first night. Psalm 34:18 for the guilt. Psalm 30:2 during recovery, said as a hope. Romans 8:1 if you were driving. And a doctor’s attention if the second keeps replaying.

faq.q: Why did God let this happen?
faq.a: Jesus was asked a version of this about a tower that fell on eighteen people (Luke 13:4). He did not give a reason. He said they were no worse than anyone else. The Bible does not explain accidents; it promises presence in them and refuses to make them a verdict. I’d be careful of anyone who offers you more than that.

faq.q: It was my fault. Is there anything for me?
faq.a: Romans 8:1, and it is not a technicality. Then a counselor, and if there is someone to make amends to, a way to do it. The Bible is full of people who caused harm and were not defined by it; that is the story, not the exception.

faq.q: What can I send someone after a car accident?
faq.a: Psalm 46:1 with: “So glad you’re here. I’m driving you to your appointments this month; just tell me when.”

title: Bible Verses When You Feel Like a Failure
h1: Bible verses when you feel like a failure
label: Feeling like a failure
for: someone who feels like a failure
description: Bible verses for the sense that you have failed at work, at marriage, at faith, or at life: Peter after the rooster, Elijah under the tree.
intent: The person feels they have failed, at a job, a marriage, parenting, faith, or life in general. They want something honest, not a pep talk, and not more pressure.
intro: The Bible keeps its failures in. Peter denies Jesus three times and is the first one Jesus goes looking for. Elijah wins the biggest contest of his life and then sits under a tree asking to die. David, Moses, Jonah, Paul: every one of them has a chapter they would have cut. These verses are for the day you feel like the sum of your worst moments. They will not tell you that you didn’t fail. They will tell you what happens after.
safety: If the failure feeling has become “everyone would be better off without me,” that is not failure talking; that is depression, and it is treatable. Please tell someone today, or call or text 988 in the US. You matter more than the thing you think you failed at.

verses.why: Jesus to Peter, hours before Peter denies him: “I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. When once you have turned again, establish your brothers.” Read that sentence slowly. Jesus knows the failure is coming, has already prayed through it, and is already assigning Peter the job he will do afterward. The failure is in the plan. So is the after.

After the resurrection, Jesus finds Peter and asks three times, “Do you love me?” One for each denial. He does not bring up the denials. He gives Peter three chances to say the opposite, and then gives him the work back. This is what restoration looks like in the Bible: not a lecture, a question, and a job.

Elijah, after the greatest victory of his ministry, under a broom tree: “It is enough. Now, O Yahweh, take away my life.” God’s answer is not a rebuke. It is food, sleep, and a touch, twice. If you have failed and are exhausted, the Bible’s prescription is embarrassingly practical: eat something and lie down. The rest comes after.

“I am forgotten from their hearts like a dead man. I am like broken pottery.” David, in the Bible, saying he feels like a broken thing everyone has thrown out. It is here so you know the feeling is old and has been prayed before. The psalm keeps going, and so does he.

“My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Paul asked three times for his weakness to be removed and was told no, and then said he would boast in it. Not in his strength. In the part of him that didn’t work. A failure is a weakness made public, and this verse says that is where the power shows up.

“Forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on.” Paul, who had persecuted the church to death, on what to do with a past: don’t carry it into the next mile. He doesn’t say it wasn’t real. He says he isn’t hauling it.

“There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus.” The verse to say out loud when the voice in your head has started sentencing. It does not say you didn’t do it. It says condemnation is not the verdict.

skip.ref: Proverbs 22:6 and “God helps those who help themselves”
skip.why: The proverb gets used on parents who feel they failed a child, as proof they did. The saying isn’t in the Bible at all, and it tells a person on the floor that God is waiting for them to get up first. Elijah under the tree is what actually happens: food, sleep, a touch.

whatToSay: “That’s hard, and it isn’t the whole story of you.”
“What would you say to a friend who did the exact same thing?” Let them hear their own answer.
Bring food. Elijah’s angel had it right.
Don’t say: “Everything happens for a reason,” or “You’ll get ’em next time.” The first is not in the Bible; the second is not the point.
howToUse: Luke 22:31–32 first, and read the whole conversation with Peter. 1 Kings 19 if you are exhausted; then actually eat and sleep. Romans 8:1 out loud when the sentencing starts. Philippians 3:13–14 for the next mile, not today.

faq.q: I failed at my faith. Does God still want me?
faq.a: Peter denied Jesus to his face, with cursing, and Jesus’ first errand after the resurrection was to go find him. Luke 22:32 says the failure was prayed through before it happened. Yes.

faq.q: How do I stop replaying it?
faq.a: You probably can’t stop the replay by willpower; you can refuse to narrate it. Philippians 3:13 is a decision made daily, not once. If the replay is constant and has been for weeks, a counselor can teach you tools that work faster than trying harder.

faq.q: What verse can I send someone who feels like a failure?
faq.a: Luke 22:31–32 with: “Jesus said this to Peter before Peter failed. Thinking of you. Dinner’s on me this week.”

title: Bible Verses When Your Child Is Being Bullied
h1: Bible verses when your child is being bullied
label: Child being bullied
for: a child who is being bullied, and the parent
description: Bible verses for a kid who is being bullied and for the parent: made on purpose, a refuge for the oppressed, a God who looks at the heart. For LGBTQ kids too.
intent: A child or teen is being bullied, at school or online, and the parent is frightened and angry. Or the young person is reading this themselves. They want something true about worth and safety, not a lecture on turning the other cheek.
intro: If your child is being bullied, you already know the two feelings: fury, and helplessness. If you are the kid reading this, you know a third one, which is that it starts to feel true. This page is for both of you. The Bible does not tell a bullied child to toughen up. It says God is a high tower for the oppressed, that he looks at the heart and not the outside, and that the child was made on purpose, exactly as they are. Kids who are gay, trans, or simply different are bullied more than anyone, and every word on this page is for them too, without exception.
safety: Bullying is not a rite of passage, and “ignore it” is not a plan. Tell the school in writing, keep a record, and if there are threats or the bullying is physical, involve the police. If your child has talked about not wanting to be alive, take it seriously today: call or text 988 in the US. LGBTQ young people can also reach The Trevor Project any hour at 1-866-488-7386 or by texting START to 678-678.

verses.why: “I am fearfully and wonderfully made.” Knit together, on purpose, by someone who does not make mistakes. Bullying works by convincing a kid that something about them is wrong: their body, their voice, who they are drawn to, how they dress. This verse says the opposite from the highest authority there is. It is the first thing to read to a bullied child, and it applies to every child, including the ones some adults have told otherwise.

“Man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” Samuel was about to pick the tall, impressive brother; God picked the youngest, the one left out in the field. Bullies judge the outside because that is all they can see. The verse says the one whose opinion matters is looking somewhere else entirely, and likes what he sees.

“Yahweh will be a high tower for the oppressed; a high tower in times of trouble.” A tower is where you go when someone is after you. The psalm does not say the bully will stop tomorrow. It says there is a place to run that is higher than the bully can reach, and it is open.

“But you do see trouble and grief. You consider it to take it into your hand. You help the victim and the fatherless.” The psalmist has just spent thirteen verses describing someone who preys on the weak and thinks nobody notices. Then: you do see. For a kid who has been told “nobody will believe you,” this is the answer. Somebody sees.

“When I am afraid, I will put my trust in you.” Short enough to say walking into school. Not “I am not afraid”; David wrote it while captured by enemies. Fear arrives, trust is chosen, and the sequence runs again at lunch. A kid can carry this one.

Nothing can separate you from the love of God: not death, not life, not powers, not anything created. A bully is a created thing. So is a group chat. So is a rumor. Read the list to a kid who thinks the cruelty says something about their worth; the verse says nothing on earth gets a vote.

“Open your mouth for the mute, in the cause of all who are left desolate.” This one is for the parent, the teacher, the older sibling, the kid who is watching it happen to someone else. Speaking up is the instruction, not turning away. It is also the verse to read before the meeting with the school.

skip.why: Jesus said it to adults about how to answer an insult without escalating, and it gets handed to bullied children as an instruction to keep taking it. That is not what it means, and a child should never be told to endure abuse as a spiritual exercise. Proverbs 31:8, speak up for those who can’t, is the instruction for the adults in the room.

whatToSay: To your child: “I believe you. This is not your fault, and it’s not okay. We’re going to deal with it together.”
“You were made on purpose, exactly as you are.” Say it plainly, and say it especially if the bullying is about who they are.

If your child is being bullied for being gay, trans, or different: “Nothing about who you are is wrong, and I am on your side.” Whatever you are still working out, they need to hear that sentence from you now, and it will decide whether they keep talking to you.
To the school, in writing: what happened, when, who, and what you expect to change. Keep copies.
Don’t say: “Just ignore them,” “Kids are mean,” or “What did you do?” None of them help, and the last one teaches them not to tell you next time.
howToUse: Read Psalm 139:13–14 with your child, and let them read it themselves. Give them Psalm 56:3 for the walk in. Keep Proverbs 31:8 for yourself, and act on it. If your child is LGBTQ and is being bullied, the estrangement page has a section written for you, because how this year goes is often what decides the next twenty.

faq.q: What does the Bible say about bullying?
faq.a: It has no verse with the word, and a great deal about the strong preying on the weak, all of it on the side of the weak. God is called a refuge for the oppressed, a helper of the fatherless, and someone who sees what the bully thinks is hidden. Jesus put a child in the middle of a room full of adults and said whoever receives one such child receives him.

faq.q: My child is being bullied for being gay or trans. Is there anything for them here?
faq.a: Every verse on this page, without exception, and Psalm 139 first. Kids who are LGBTQ are bullied at far higher rates and are at far higher risk of hurting themselves, and the single biggest protective factor is whether one parent is clearly on their side. Whatever your church teaches and whatever you are still working through, your child’s safety and your relationship with them come first, and nothing in Scripture requires you to choose the doctrine over the child. Tell them they were made on purpose. Mean it.

faq.q: Should my child fight back?
faq.a: That is a safety and school-policy question, not a Bible question, and this page won’t pretend otherwise. What Scripture does say is that the adults are responsible to speak up (Proverbs 31:8) and that a child should never be told to absorb abuse as a spiritual discipline.

faq.q: What verse can I send a kid who is being bullied?
faq.a: Psalm 139:14 with one line: “You were made on purpose, and I’m on your side.”
